title: Your Android phone may remember AI chats you thought you deleted
summary: Keeping your AI conversations offline doesn't necessarily mean they're gone when you delete them.
body: TL;DR Tech researchers have developed a forensic tool that recovers deleted conversations from AI apps running locally on Android devices. In one experiment, the tool recovered 26 previously shared facts, compared with just 14 accessible to the original AI session. The technique requires forensic access to device data and doesn’t establish that conversations from cloud-based chatbots are similarly recoverable. Recovering deleted information from phones is hardly a new trick. We’ve seen it with text messages , photos, and other supposedly erased data. But researchers have taken things somewhere more intriguing: they’ve developed a forensic tool that can retrieve deleted AI conversations and actually bring the chatbot back to life, complete with some of its previous knowledge. According to researchers at Georgia Tech (via Digital Trends ), the technique uses a forensic tool called ORISA to piece together information AI apps leave behind on Android phones. These local assistants process conversations on your device, offering more privacy by keeping your chats away from remote servers. body: TL;DR OpenAI introduces its latest model, GPT-6.1 Terra, with excellent cost/performance balance. While Astra is still OpenAI’s performance king, Terra can offer output quality that’s not much lower, for a mere fraction of the cost. Despite similar performance to GPT-6.1 Sol, Terra operates at roughly half the price. Progress moves so fast when it comes to all things AI, that “bigger and better” hardly even feels like the target. Instead, we find ourselves tracking developments across multiple fronts, where sometimes it’s just as impressive to find your gains in terms of efficiency — matching the performance of another model for a mere fraction of the cost. That’s exactly the sort of momentum we’re looking at from OpenAI today, as the company shares GPT-6.1 Terra. It’s coming up on a month now since we got to meet GPT-6.1 Sol , and today OpenAI introduces its next model to cross the 6.1 threshold, with GPT-6.1 Terra. title: Ultrahuman pushes back against Oura’s bid to ban the Ring Pro
summary: The legal battle is just getting started.
body: TL;DR Ultrahuman has responded to the lawsuit filed by Oura alleging that the Ring Pro violates two of its patents. The company has rejected the patent infringement claims and says it will respond through legal channels. Oura filed its lawsuit in a Texas federal court last week, seeking a ban on Ring Pro sales in addition to monetary damages. Oura has filed multiple lawsuits against rival smart ring manufacturers, and even secured a ban on the Ultrahuman Ring Air over a patent dispute in 2025. Fast forward to last week, when the company filed a new federal lawsuit alleging that Ultrahuman’s newer model, the Ring Pro, violates two Oura patents , and the smart ring manufacturer is once again staring down the threat of a ban. Ultrahuman has now responded to the allegations, reiterating claims made by the co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar last week. In an extended statement shared with Android Authority , Ultrahuman says it remains confident in the Ring Pro and that it “represents a substantially redesigned generation” of the company’s tech. The manufacturer adds that the US Customs and Border Protection found no violation of Oura’s patents mentioned in the Ring Air lawsuit last year.

body: Most Android users don’t bother considering browsers beyond Google Chrome , and why would they? It’s quick, it’s stable, and it’ll likely load any web page you throw at it. Why fix something that isn’t broken? However, for power users who aim to rid their phones of big tech influence, there’s a problem: the Google part of that equation. Since it’s Android’s default browser, Chrome is laced with all sorts of Google infusions and limitations. The company has battled against ad-blocking extensions on desktop, while somehow still keeping extension support off of official mobile builds. title: I canceled Google AI Plus after the downgrade, but I’m still using Gemini
summary: I won't let Google fool me again.
body: I’ve been a Gemini user for a couple of years now. I use it mainly for learning new skills and summarizing concepts. It’s well-integrated with whatever Android smartphone I use, giving me helpful features like Circle to Search and Gemini Live. I’ve experimented with other AI chatbots, but none of them are as straightforward and accessible as Gemini. I decided to subscribe to Google AI Plus earlier this year. It served two purposes: provide me a higher usage allowance for Gemini and increase my shared Google One storage to 400GB. For $5 a month, it seemed like a great deal at first. After all, that’s arguably the biggest reason to buy a fitness tracker , and with the Edge costing $80 more than the Air, I wanted to know whether you’re actually getting better health features or just paying extra for a screen.

title: Which phone has the best portrait camera mode? I tested the big three to find out

Getting all three right, however, is easier said than done, and smartphone makers have very different ideas about how to achieve it. To find out which approach works best, I grabbed my iPhone, the latest Google Pixel 11 Pro XL , and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus for a head-to-head comparison. If you want to make the Gemini app more useful, you could start using Connected Apps. These are apps that can be integrated with the chatbot, allowing you to access their services without leaving your Gemini conversation. Recently , Peloton, SeatGeek, Airtable, and others have become Connected Apps, but Google is far from done. Another useful app just joined the Connected App collection.
